summary: Defines a framework for preconditions in SIP, extensible through IANA registration, and shows how network quality of service can be a precondition for starting a session. Participants reserve network resources before the call proceeds. It does not define new reservation mechanisms. It was later updated by RFCs 4032 and 5027.

eli5.summary: Before a phone rings, both sides make sure the road is clear and a lane is reserved. This document lets a call wait until the network promises enough room.

questions: how does sip work with quality of service reservation
what is a ghost ring in sip
what do a=curr and a=des mean in sdp
subtitle: How a SIP call can wait to ring the phone until the network has promised enough bandwidth.

tldr.problem: Reserving network resources needs the callee's address, port and session parameters, which only arrive in the first offer/answer exchange, and that exchange normally makes the callee's phone ring. Resources cannot be reserved before ringing, and ringing should not happen before resources are reserved.
tldr.mechanism: The caller adds preconditions to the SDP offer: current-status, desired-status and confirm-status attributes per media stream. The callee answers but does not alert the user until every mandatory precondition is met.
tldr.outcome: Sessions can be set up with few 'ghost rings', because the callee is only alerted once the reservation has succeeded. The RFC defines the framework and the 'qos' precondition type, not new reservation mechanisms.

today: RFC 3312 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 4032 and RFC 5027. Read those together with this document for the full picture.

sections.title: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
sections.content:
Some architectures want the chance of failure to be minimal once the callee has been alerted. One source of failure is being unable to reserve network resources for the session. To minimize ghost rings, resources should be reserved before the callee is alerted.

The catch is that reserving resources usually requires the IP address, port and session parameters of the callee. Those come from the initial offer/answer exchange in SIP, and that exchange normally causes the phone to ring. Resources cannot be reserved without the exchange, and the exchange cannot happen without the reservation.

The way out is a precondition: a set of constraints about the session, introduced in the offer. The recipient answers but does not alert the user or continue session establishment until the preconditions are met. That can be learned from a local event, such as confirmation of a reservation, or from a new offer sent by the caller. The preconditions live in the SDP description rather than in a SIP header, because they are specific to each media stream.
sections.eli5: You cannot book a table without knowing the restaurant, and you cannot go to the restaurant without a table. So you phone ahead, agree on the booking, and only then walk in.

sections.title: Current Status and Desired Status
sections.content:
For each media stream the RFC tracks two state variables: current status and desired status. The desired status is a threshold for the current status. Session establishment stops until the current status reaches or surpasses that threshold, then it resumes.

For example, if resources are reserved only in the send direction but both directions are desired, establishment does not resume. If resources are reserved in both directions (sendrecv) and only the send direction is desired, it does.

These variables are exchanged in the offer/answer model of RFC 3264 like any other SDP media attribute, such as the direction attribute or the codecs in use. That gives both user agents a shared view of the stream.

In the basic flow, caller A puts quality of service preconditions in the INVITE. B agrees, handles reservation in the B to A direction, and asks A to handle the other direction and confirm. B answers in a 183 (Session Progress) response. When A finishes, it sends an UPDATE, B replies 200 (OK) to show the preconditions are met, and only then does B alert the user.
sections.eli5: There are two scoreboards: what you have so far and what you need. The call only goes ahead once the first is at least as big as the second.

sections.title: The SDP Attributes
sections.content:
The RFC defines three media-level SDP attributes: a=curr (current status), a=des (desired status) and a=conf (confirmation status). Each carries a precondition type, a status type and a direction tag. The desired-status attribute also has a strength tag.

  • Precondition type: qos in this document. Extensions may define others.
  • Status type: e2e for an end-to-end reservation, or local and remote for the segmented case, where each user agent reserves in its own access network.
  • Direction tag: none, send, recv or sendrecv.
  • Strength tag: mandatory, optional, none, plus failure and unknown used when refusing an offer.

The tags send, recv, local and remote are from the point of view of whoever generated the SDP. In an offer, send means offerer to answerer. In an answer it means answerer to offerer.

The confirm-status attribute is a threshold: when the status of network resources reaches it, the peer sends an updated session description with a new current status.
sections.eli5: It is a little form with boxes to tick: what kind of promise, which direction, and how badly you need it.

sections.title: Offers, Answers and Status Tables
sections.content:
To keep both sides in step, the RFC models three tables: each user agent keeps a local status table, and each offer/answer exchange has a transaction status table. The offerer builds the transaction table from its local table and sends it in the offer. The answerer uses it to update its own table, fixes anything out of date and returns it in the answer. Afterwards both local tables agree. This is a model of behavior, not of software.

The strength tags are ordered none, optional, mandatory. An answerer MAY upgrade a strength but MUST NOT downgrade it. So a caller that supports preconditions but does not need them can send none and the answerer can still ask for a reservation without another round trip.

The meanings are: none needs no reservation, optional means the agents SHOULD try but the session can continue anyway, and mandatory means they MUST provide it or session establishment MUST NOT continue.

In the encoding, equal strengths in both directions are written as one sendrecv line. Different strengths need separate send and recv lines. In the answer the tags are inverted: send becomes recv, and local becomes remote.
sections.eli5: Both people keep a checklist and swap copies. You may mark something as more important, but you may never say it matters less than the other person did.

sections.title: Suspending, Resuming and Confirming
sections.content:
A user agent server that receives an offer with preconditions SHOULD NOT alert the user until all the mandatory preconditions are met. Meanwhile user agents SHOULD NOT send data on any media stream; for RTP, neither RTP nor RTCP packets are sent. It knows the preconditions are met for a stream when its local table says yes in every row marked mandatory. When all media lines are satisfied, establishment SHOULD resume.

A server that cannot meet all mandatory preconditions on its own MUST include a conf attribute in the SDP it sends. When the threshold in that attribute is reached or crossed again, the receiver MUST send a new offer with the updated current status. Confirmation attributes are not negotiated.

The same rules apply in the middle of a session: both sides keep using the old session parameters until the mandatory preconditions are met, and only then switch to the new ones. The RFC's example is a caller changing the IP address where it receives media.

An offerer MUST put the option tag precondition in a Require header field when any strength is mandatory. Otherwise it goes in Supported or Require, with Supported RECOMMENDED. A user agent using preconditions MUST support PRACK and UPDATE.
sections.eli5: The phone stays quiet until everything on the list is checked off. If you cannot check something off yourself, you ask the other side to shout when it is ready.

sections.title: Refusing an Offer
sections.content:
The RFC adds a new SIP status code, 580 (Precondition Failure). An answerer that cannot or will not meet the preconditions SHOULD reject the offer with it. When an offer arrives in a 1xx or 2xx response, SIP has no way to refuse it, so the receiver answers correctly and then sends a CANCEL or BYE.

A 580 response, BYE or CANCEL SHOULD carry an SDP description showing which desired status caused the failure. It is not an offer or answer. It must have the same number of m= lines as the last SDP received, each with port zero, and the failing line uses the strength tag failure.

A user agent that gets a mandatory precondition of an unknown type MUST refuse the offer, using the tag unknown, unless the only unknown mandatory preconditions have the local tag. A stream whose port is set to zero is rejected as usual, and its preconditions are ignored.
sections.eli5: If you cannot keep the promise being asked for, you say so clearly and point at exactly which part you cannot do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An entity in the middle could add desired-status attributes that make session establishment impossible. It could also edit current-status values so the session starts without the preconditions being met. Integrity protection can be used against both attacks.

An entity that reserves resources in response to unauthenticated requests with preconditions is an easy target for denial of service. Requests with preconditions SHOULD be authenticated.

For IANA, the RFC registers the three SDP attributes, the 580 status code and the precondition option tag, and sets up a registry of precondition types where qos is the only entry.
sections.eli5: Someone in the middle could tamper with the checklist, or trick you into saving lots of seats for people who never show up. So check who is asking and make sure the note is not altered.

data.title: Initial offer SDP1
data.code:
m=audio 20000 RTP/AVP 0
c=IN IP4 192.0.2.1
a=curr:qos e2e none
a=des:qos mandatory e2e sendrecv
